response.title: what home battery backup should i buy for power outages if i cant use a gas generator
response.answer:
If you can't use a gas generator, I recommend a LiFePO₄ (LFP) home battery backup. It's quiet, produces no exhaust, can operate indoors, and can keep essential appliances running during a power outage.

The best choice depends on whether you want to power just your refrigerator, internet, and lights, or keep most of your house running.

There are two main options:

Portable power stations: Typically $1,000–$5,000+ depending on capacity. No permanent installation required. Best for renters, apartments, and essential appliances.

Whole-home battery systems: Typically $10,000–$25,000+ installed, depending on capacity and electrical work. Best for homeowners who want automatic backup during outages.

My top battery recommendations
Shop

1. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3

Best overall for essentials

4.1 kWh · 4,000W · 120/240V

My first choice for a refrigerator, internet, lights, and several small appliances. Expandable and supports home electrical integration.

Better for higher-power appliances and future expansion. One unit can support up to six additional battery packs.

3. Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus

5.04 kWh · 7,200W · 120/240V

A strong option if you need more inverter output and capacity in a single unit, particularly for larger household loads.

View product

Shop

4. EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra

6.14 kWh per battery · 7,200W per inverter

Best of these for a more permanent, expandable home backup setup. Requires compatible electrical integration for automatic home backup.

Inverter + battery listing: $4,199.00

View system

How long will a battery last?

Here's an example assuming you are powering a refrigerator, Wi-Fi, a few LED lights, and small electronics, averaging 200 watts combined.

4.1 kWh — EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3
10 kWh — expanded battery system

Estimated runtime

17.4 hours
Assumes 85% usable AC energy after conversion losses. Actual runtime varies with appliance cycling, temperature, and battery condition.

A battery that can run a refrigerator and Wi-Fi for most of a day may only run an electric space heater for a couple of hours. Capacity (kWh) determines runtime; output (W) determines what appliances can run simultaneously.

For outages lasting several days, solar charging or significantly more battery capacity becomes important.

What I'd buy

For a typical home where the goal is to survive a 12–24-hour outage without running air conditioning or electric heating, I'd start with the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, then add capacity if needed.

For automatic backup of wired household circuits, I'd look at a professionally installed battery system or an expandable portable system with a compatible transfer switch. Never connect a power station to a house outlet to backfeed the wiring.

One important consideration: a battery is not a generator. Once depleted, it needs grid power, solar, or another charging source.

Essentials plus cooking and other appliances
Most of the house, including heating or AC
3. How long should backup last?
8 hours

48 hours
3 days or longer
Find the right battery for me

These answers will help determine whether a $1,000–$3,000 portable system is enough or whether you need a much larger home battery installation.
